source_text: Ubi autem de Christo dicitur: Qui sanctificat, et sanctificatur ex uno omnes [n112] , non de Adam, sed de Deo accipi potest, cuius virtute Christus secundum carnem factus est et omne humanum genus; ac per hoc ad labefactandam intellegentiam Apostoli, qua dixit per unum hominem peccatum intrasse in mundum, aliorum similitudo verborum nihil quivit afferre momenti. Haereat tamen id, quod sequitur, maxime prudentis animo lectoris, ut intellegat me hactenus multo remissius, quam res postulabat, egisse. Patiamur quippe, ut plurimis testimoniis doceatur generationem, quae nisi per duos fieri non potest, agi tamen etiam per unum solere dici. Verum nihil opinio traducis promovebit: cur? Videlicet quia alia sunt, quae abusive, alia, quae proprie dicimus. Ergo ea, quae sunt propria, appellationes suas sine dispendio largiuntur; ea vero, quae per usurpationem dicuntur, principalibus rebus videlicet propriis definitionum suarum praeiudicia non sinuntur invehere; fitque hoc totum inculpabiliter, cum rebus, de quibus non est ulla dubitatio, per abusionem vocabula impertimur aliena.
pass_a_gloss: But where it is said of Christ: He who sanctifies, and he is sanctified, all from one, it can be taken not of Adam but of God, by whose power Christ according to the flesh was made and the whole human race; and through this the similarity of other words could bring nothing of moment to weakening the understanding of the Apostle, by which he said that through one human sin entered into the world. Let that nevertheless which follows cling especially to the mind of the prudent reader, that he understand that thus far I have acted much more remissly than the matter was demanding. Let us indeed suffer that by very many testimonies it be taught that generation, which unless through two cannot be done, is nevertheless accustomed to be said to be done even through one. But the opinion of the vine-layer will promote nothing: why? Namely because some things we say abusively, others properly. Therefore those which are proper lavish their appellations without loss; but those which are said by usurpation are not allowed to bring in prejudices of their definitions upon principal things, namely their proper ones; and this whole happens inculpably, when to things about which there is not any doubt we impart by abuse alien vocabula.

lemmas.lexica: LS tradux=vine-shoot/layer; Blaise tradux peccati=transmission of sin by descent
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin

pass_b_english: Where it is said of Christ, ‘The one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one’ (Hebrews 2:11) (Romans 5:12), this can be understood as referring not to Adam but to God, by whose power Christ according to the flesh and the whole human race were made. Consequently, the similarity of other expressions has contributed nothing to undermine the apostle’s meaning when he said that sin entered the world through one man.

Yet what follows should stay firmly in the sensible reader’s mind: understand that so far I have argued far more leniently than the matter required. Let us allow that many testimonies show generation, which cannot happen except through two, is nevertheless commonly said to occur through one. The theory of inherited sin will still gain nothing. Why? Because some expressions are figurative or extended, and others are proper and exact. Things with proper names can lend their terms without suffering loss. But things spoken of in a borrowed sense are not allowed to impose the implications of their own definitions on the primary things to which the terms properly belong. All this happens without fault when we lend words to matters about which there is no doubt.

choices.why: Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)

choices.why: For Julian, sin requires rational choice; infants lack usus rationis.
